messages.subject: Re: Summary Fit Display on CFA
messages.subject_clean: Summary Fit Display on CFA
messages.body_plain:
Valerie,
  The other packages are not disabling the cfa() function but merely masking it.  To see how that works, try the following.

F # R returns FALSE
F <- TRUE # Masks the native F with a user assigned object of the same name
F # R returns TRUE
rm(F) # unmask the native F by deleting the user defined F
F # R returns FALSE again.

  So, the lavaan cfa() function is always there, it is just that R is looking for a cfa() function somewhere other than lavaan first, and using the first one that it finds.

  The foo::bar idiom is a form of defensive programming that always explicitly tells R where to look.  That way, the code will work no mater what you load in what order.

  If you do not like that idiom, you can avoid the problem by always listing lavaan last when you load your dependencies.  R will look for things from most recently loaded to least recently loaded.  However, this approach will not work if (a) you need two functions the names of which are shared between two packages and (b) you need one from each pair from each of the two packages.  That does not happen very often, but if it does you will need to use the explicit idiom or, alternatively, detach packages not currently being used.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

sorry to jump on the older thread, but I'll try my luck, as I also have issues with multiple imputation with lavaan and semTools.

I have installed the following versions of lavaan and semTools (I was kindly directed to another post in this group by one of the stackoverflow members):

install.packages("lavaan", repos = "http://www.da.ugent.be", type = "source")

# if necessary:    install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("simsem/semTools/semTools")

Then I run my model:
model5 <- 'zceadiff ~ mompa + zcdpea + momabhx
mompa ~ b1*zpeadiff + c*momabhx + b2*zmommhpsi
zpeadiff ~ a1*momabhx
zcdpea ~ momabhx
zmommhpsi ~ a2*momabhx
zpeadiff ~~ zcdpea
direct := c
indirect1 := a1 * b1
indirect1 := a2 * b2
total    := c + (a1 * b1) + (a2 * b2)'

fit5 <- runMI(model5, data = imputedData, fun="sem", ordered = "mompa", estimator="WLSMV")
summary(fit5, standardized = TRUE, ci = T)

It runs fine, except if I add "chi" = "mplus" to the runMI statement. Then it returns:   lavaan ERROR: unknown argument 'chi'
I've looked at semTools documentation and tried all over possible combinations to get fit indices for my model, from lavInspect or lavListInspect to fitMeasuresMX, with no result.

It does work if I use the solution posted in the end of this thread, anova(fit5, indices=T), but is there a way to get the original "chi=mplus" statement to work and get the model fit measures printed in a fashion similar to lavaan?

Thank you!!
Best,
Maria

messages.subject: Re: Saturated model - How to address in lavaan / proceed and write up results/discussion?
messages.subject_clean: Saturated model - How to address in lavaan / proceed and write up results/discussion?
messages.body_plain:
If the model you want to assess has zero df,  you can still report the parameter estimates.

It's not really a limitation that you can't assess model fit. Every regression, correlation, anova, ancova, etc model also has zero df and fit can't be assessed. (And every multilevel model might not fit, but there's no such thing as a saturated model in multilevel models, so the fit also can't be assessed).

Jeremy

messages.body_plain:
I am trying to work on a model based on moderator variable 'C'. The code is as follows.

model1 <- '
BE=~BE1+BE2+BE3+BE4+BE5
BA=~BA1+BA2+BA3+BA4+BA5+BA6
BAS=~BAS1+BAS2+BAS3+BAS4+BAS5+BAS6+BAS7+BAS8+BAS9
PQ=~PQ1+PQ2+PQ3+PQ4+PQ5+PQ6+PQ7+PQ8+PQ9+PQ10
L=~L1+L2+L3+L4+L5+L6+L7
INF=~INF1+INF2+INF3+INF4
C=~C1+C2+C3+C4+C5+C6+C7+C8+C9+C10

PQC=~PQ+C+PQ*C
BE=~BA+PQC+BAS+L+INF
'
nBoots <- 1000
fit1 <- lavaan::sem(model1, data=DSem, se = "boot", test = "Bollen.Stine", bootstrap = nBoots)
lavaan::parameterEstimates(fit1, boot.ci.type = "norm", standardized = TRUE)
lavaan::summary(fit1, standardized=TRUE)

The bootstrap always hangs . How much time it should take? Is there any other way to bypass a negative variance situation. The variable PQC is having a negative value and therefore I am trying to use the bootstrap command.

Thanks & regards,

messages.subject: Re: The bootstrap is hanging for SEM
messages.subject_clean: The bootstrap is hanging for SEM
messages.body_plain:
That's a big model. If your sample size is large, then bootstrapping will take a while. If your sample size is not large, then I suspect that the model is struggling to converge, at least some of the time, and reaching the iteration limit. The models that reach the iteraction limit could take quite a while (a minute or two?).

Try nBoots <- 1, then 10, then 100, etc.  This should give you some idea of how long it will take.

(In regard to a bootstrap analysis with Mplus, someone asked why the model was hanging - even though it had been running for a couple of hourse. Linda Muthen suggested getting back to them if it took longer than 3 days.)

Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: The bootstrap is hanging for SEM
messages.subject_clean: The bootstrap is hanging for SEM
messages.body_plain:
Hello.

Ed, Terrance and others can certainly offer you a more complete response but let me drop a quick comment on your question:

The asterisk '*' is used to label estimates/parameters. For example, if you have, say,

y ~ LAB*x1

a label 'LAB' will be attached to the parameter estimate. If your syntax is like

y ~ LAB*x1
LAB == 2

you'd be constraining the coefficient for x1 to be equal to 2; on the other hand,  if you have something like

y ~ LAB*x1
LAB < 1.75

you'd be constraining the parameter estimate for x1 to be lesser than 1.75.

If I am getting it correctly, if one has a syntax like

PQC=~PQ+C+PQ*C

the model is simply 'PQC=~PQ+C+C' -- but your attaching a 'PQ' label to the second C variable. As far as I get it, lavaan automatically drops repeated indicators for latent variables. All in all, 'PQC=~PQ+C+PQ*C' boils down to 'PQC=~PQ+C'.

Take a look at the output for this silly example:

library(lavaan)

HS.model1 <- ' x1 ~ x4 + x2 + x4*x2'

fit1 <- lavaan(HS.model1, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
              auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,
              auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE)
summary(fit1, fit.measures=TRUE)

As you'll see, lavaan will assumed that, in 'x4*x2', 'x4' is simply the label for the second 'x2' in the syntax; therefore, it will take that x4 has been (mistakenly) entered twice in the model syntax and  will drop one of the x2 from it.  The model will actually be reduced to 'x1 ~ x4 + x2'.

Therefore, a syntax like 'PQC=~PQ+C+PQ*C' might not be appropriate for a moderation/mediation analysis as intended by diya.

To perform a mediation analysis in lavaan, it is necessary to "define" new parameters using the ":=" operator. Yves provides one example at http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/mediation.html

messages.body_plain:
I am building a PA model using lavaan using a sample size of 63000 records with non-normal categorical binary and ordinal variables.

Probably by this sample size, after the model estimation we obtained a high chi-square result and insignificant p-value.

So I would like to confirm some assumptions I got after reading some literature:
The X2 test is sensisitve by the large sample sizes and would be corrected, it the normality assumptions are not valid, using Satorra Bentler correction.
If correct, in lavaan we can fix it using test="Satorra.Bentler" in lavaan ?

In Kline book (2015) page 80, the use of normed chi-­square (x2/df) is discourage because X2 is sensitive to sample size only for incorrect models; df has nothing to do with sample size and there were really never any “acceptable” clear-cut guidelines about maximum values of the normed chi-­square (e.g., < 2.0?—< 3.0?).
So I have seem a lot of papers using this index. Should I use it when evaluating the quality of my model or not?

Even with the satorra bentler correction the X2 is most likely to reject the null hypothesis.

There is no research that shows that the X2/df works, under any condition. I havent seen papers using it but they shouldnt.

For this assesing of model fit (quality) is recommended to use other fit indexes, such as CFI, TLI, RMSEA, gamma-hat, Mc. The function fitMeasures of lavaan and moreFitindices from semTools provide plenty of fit indexes.

>From research it shows that gamma-hat, RMSEA, and MC to have better behavior

You can check

West, S. G., Taylor, A. B., & Wu, W. (2012). Model fit and model selection in structural equation modeling. In R. H. Hoyle (Ed.), Handbook of Structural Equation Modeling (pp. 209-231). New York, NY: Guilford.

Fan, Xitao and Sivo, Stephen A.(2007) 'Sensitivity of Fit Indices to Model Misspecification and Model Types', Multivariate Behavioral Research, 42: 3, 509 — 529

Hello,
I try to evaluate a theoretical CFA model. I am generating the samples with the simsem <https://github.com/simsem/simsem/wiki/Example-1:-Getting-Started> package according to the following model:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-0CDBxcVkwFQ/Wk6vY3ejwwI/AAAAAAAAEjU/Uxs7-jlu1d0QcBLww9rwjJ_woPHmYjjQgCLcBGAs/s1600/Screenshot_1.png>
data <- generate(CFA.Model,200) #Generate a sample of multivariate normal distribution

Then I transform the data to categorical variables with the following function:

DichoData <- function(data,q){
D <- data.frame(ifelse (data < apply(data,2,quantile,q),0,1))
return(D)
}

With the implementation of the lavaan package, the model is as follows:

Model <- "
f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3
f2 =~ y4 + y5 + y6
f1 ~~ f2
"

# With original data
fit.1 <- cfa(model = Model, data = data, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

To implement the model with categorical variables, the "order" argument is added:

# With categorical data
fit.2 <- cfa(model = Model, data = DichoData(data,0.5), std.lv <http://std.lv> = T, order = names(data))

However, the model is estimated with DWLS. I would like to run the model with "ML", "WLS" or "ULS". The question is: Could I evaluate the model with the matrix of tetrachoric correlations? like this:

# Alternative
require(psych)
fit.3 <- cfa(model = Model, sample.cov = tetrachoric(DichoData(data,0.5))$rho,
sample.nobs = 200, std.lv <http://std.lv> = T, estimator = "ML")

fit.4 <- cfa(model = Model, sample.cov = tetrachoric(DichoData(data,0.5))$rho,
sample.nobs = 200, std.lv <http://std.lv> = T, estimator = "ULS")

fit.5 <- cfa(model = Model, sample.cov = tetrachoric(DichoData(data,0.5))$rho,
sample.nobs = 200, std.lv <http://std.lv> = T, estimator = "WLS")

The fit.3 and fit.4 models converge without problems, and the estimates of the parameters of the model are acceptable. The fit.5 model does not work because it needs the weight matrix.
Is it reasonable to assume that if the results are similar, then the method is acceptable?

Thanks for your attention.

messages.subject: Re: Chi-square result for large sample size and normed chi-square
messages.subject_clean: Chi-square result for large sample size and normed chi-square
messages.body_plain:
Elias,
  It is somewhat misleading to say that chi-square is sensitive to N.  It is not that the large N makes the chi-square inaccurate in some way.  However, you may have sufficient power to detect trivial discrepancies between the observed and implied moments.  The correction for non-normality is not related to having a large N and the chi-square is not in need of any correction for having a large N.

  My suggestion in such circumstances would be to pay special attention to the residuals in a correlation metric.  In the correlation metric, you can think about how big a difference in correlations is of any practical significance.  Then look at the residuals and see how many, if any, exceed that threshold.  If none do, then you can report that the chi-square indicated an overall difference but that all of the differences were too small to be of practical significance.

   What makes the ratio of chi-square to df interesting is that the df are the mean of the chi-quare distribution.  So, some of us take chi-square < df as a potential warning that a model is at risk for overfitting the sample.  However, given that the shape of the distribution changes with df, it is hard to give any meaningful interpretation to the ratio when it exceeds 1.

  Whatever you do, bear in mind that there are no universally accepted practices.  Kline's overview of model evaluation is very good, at least for those of us who take a holistic perspective on model evaluation.  When you report your results, clearly connect the dots between your conclusions and the evidence that you provide to support them.  Be sure to provide sufficient information that the reader can make his or her own independent evaluation.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject_clean: Estimation CFA of Categorical Data without "DWLS"
messages.body_plain:
> according to the following model:

Your arrows should point in the other direction for factor loadings.  The factor explains the indicators, not vice versa.

> Then I transform the data to categorical variables with the following function:
>
> DichoData <- function(data,q){
> D <- data.frame(ifelse (data < apply(data,2,quantile,q),0,1))
> return(D)
> }

That means your threshold is not a population parameter, because it changes from sample to sample.

> To implement the model with categorical variables, the "order" argument is added:

That should be  ordered

> However, the model is estimated with DWLS. I would like to run the model with "ML", "WLS" or "ULS".

Then you cannot trust your SEs or test statistics from ML or ULS.  DWLS is used instead of WLS because the inverting the weight matrix becomes unstable with more than a couple variables (especially with such a small sample of 200) and eventually intractable with more than a few variables.

> The question is: Could I evaluate the model with the matrix of tetrachoric correlations? like this:

Yes, but only your point estimates would be unbiased (see comment above about SEs and tests).  You can also use lavCor() in the lavaan package instead of additionally depending on the psych package.

> The fit.3 and fit.4 models converge without problems, and the estimates of the parameters of the model are acceptable. The fit.5 model does not work because it needs the weight matrix.

lavCor() can return a fitted lavaan model for estimating the tetrachorics (and thresholds).  See the ?lavCor help page, bottom example.  So you could construct the weight matrix from the vcov() output of that model for tetrachorics.  I think you could omit the thresholds part of that matrix, since your input data is just the matrix of tetrachoric correlations.

> Is it reasonable to assume that if the results are similar, then the method is acceptable?

The benchmark is not consistency across estimators, but each estimator's consistency with the true population parameters.  As I pointed out above, your threshold should probably be a parameter (e.g., zero) instead of a sample quantile.

messages.body_plain:
> can I still use multiple groups LGM to fit the data

Yes.  Mplus and the R package OpenMx have ways to specify individual-specific factor loadings, so you could specify a different time-pattern for each country (but use the same pattern for all individuals within a country).   Alternatively, you could use the mixed-modeling approach (e.g., in the nlme or lme4 packages) instead of SEM to estimate the growth curve, handling multiple groups by means of interaction between time and group-dummy codes.

> can I use lavaan to do the analysis?

I think the only way to do this in lavaan would be to structure your data as though they were balanced, and simply have missing values (NA) for time periods not observed within a particular group.  If the data are continuous, you can use FIML to handle missing data.

If you want to use another method described above, you can ask for help  on SEMNET:

www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html <http://www2.gsu.edu/~mkteer/semnet.html>

messages.body_plain:
> 1. How to interpret the coefficients of my final regression. Ideally, I would like to use logistic regression so that I could interpret the coefficient of g and item11 as odds ratios. Can I?

No, lavaan sets link = "probit" by default, but there is an experimental link = "logit" option you could try (see ?lavOptions).  Logit transforms probabilities into log-odds, whereas probit transforms probabilities into z-scores from a standard normal distribution (e.g., a probability of 50% is associated with a z-score of 0, and probability of 84% is associated with a z-score of 1).  So you can interpret your effects as changes in units of SD for the transformed outcome variable.

This is equivalent to assuming there is a normally distributed "latent item response" underlying the binary outcome, although that might not make sense if the variable is truly dichotomous rather than a supposedly continuous construct that is simply measured with a binary scale.  You can read more about this here:

http://dx.doi.org/10.1207/S15327906347-387

http://dx.doi.org/10.1080/10705510701758406

> 2. What does this mean, it is given in the output?
>
> Scales y*:
>                    Estimate  Std.Err  z-value  P(>|z|)   Std.lv  Std.all
>     binary01    1.000                               1.000    1.000

This is the SD of the latent item response, described above.

> 3. When I use lavaan() the model does not really run

This is probably because your model syntax does not specify all model parameters, particularly for the categorical outcome that you are unfamiliar with (e.g., a threshold).  Using the sem() function turns on some sensible defaults.  You can see what they are from your sem() output:

dfit@call

> I can't assume a continuous construct that was measured on a binary scale. We are measuring a behavior that either individuals did or did not perform.

That does not matter, you can still use the probit link.  It is just an arbitrary transformation.  Any book on categorical data analysis will tell you that results from logistic and probit regression area almost always nearly identical (e.g., see p. 70 at the link below)

https://mregresion.files.wordpress.com/2012/08/agresti-introduction-to-categorical-data.pdf

> I tried the experimental link="logit" but it did not work:

As I said, it is only experimental, so you should just use the probit regression.

> Maybe because I ran it in sem() and not lavaan(). Does it not work in sem()? (I got the same output as without the link="logit" using sem())

sem() is just a wrapper around lavaan() with certain defaults turned on (see ?lavOptions), so the same arguments apply to both.

> could you expand on what dfit@call means?

You "call" an R function.  The following is a call to the round() function, with 2 arguments

round(pi, digits = 2)

A lavaan object saves the call to lavaan() in a "slot", that you access using the @ operator.  So dfit@call simply shows you what the lavaan() call looked like when you used the sem() function (which calls lavaan() with certain defaults set).  From the ?cfa help page:

              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit@call # if you evaluate this call, you get the same result

               model.type = "cfa", int.ov.free = TRUE, int.lv.free = FALSE,
               auto.fix.first = TRUE, auto.fix.single = TRUE, auto.var = TRUE,
               auto.cov.lv.x = TRUE, auto.cov.y = TRUE, auto.th <http://auto.th> = TRUE,
               auto.delta = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
Ann,
An SE model can only have one equation for each variable.  When you include multiple equation in your model syntax, lavaan needs to combine these into one equation.  If you tell lavaan that Y ~ c*X+d*Cov and Y ~ b*M then lavaan can just combine these into one equation Y ~ c*X+d*Cov + b*M.  However, if you tell lavaan that Y ~ c*X+d*Cov
and Y ~ b*M +g*Cov then putting these together yields Y ~ c*X+d*Cov + b*M +g*Cov.  It is not possible to estimate two separate weights for Cov.  Those are the duplicate elements that lavaan is complaining about.

Y and M are both endogenous variables in your model.  So, each has its own equation and its own R-square.

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

> Elias,
>   It is somewhat misleading to say that chi-square is sensitive to N.  It is not that the large N makes the chi-square inaccurate in some way.  However, you may have sufficient power to detect trivial discrepancies between the observed and implied moments.  The correction for non-normality is not related to having a large N and the chi-square is not in need of any correction for having a large N.
>
>   My suggestion in such circumstances would be to pay special attention to the residuals in a correlation metric.  In the correlation metric, you can think about how big a difference in correlations is of any practical significance.  Then look at the residuals and see how many, if any, exceed that threshold.  If none do, then you can report that the chi-square indicated an overall difference but that all of the differences were too small to be of practical significance.
>
>    What makes the ratio of chi-square to df interesting is that the df are the mean of the chi-quare distribution.  So, some of us take chi-square < df as a potential warning that a model is at risk for overfitting the sample.  However, given that the shape of the distribution changes with df, it is hard to give any meaningful interpretation to the ratio when it exceeds 1.
>
>   Whatever you do, bear in mind that there are no universally accepted practices.  Kline's overview of model evaluation is very good, at least for those of us who take a holistic perspective on model evaluation.  When you report your results, clearly connect the dots between your conclusions and the evidence that you provide to support them.  Be sure to provide sufficient information that the reader can make his or her own independent evaluation.

messages.subject: Re: identification SEM model
messages.subject_clean: identification SEM model
messages.body_plain:
Michelle--
     Counting DF can be tricky, because you will eitehr have some loadings fixed or else some factor variances fixed, in order to "scale" each factor. DF need to be counted for the whole model, though you also need to know that each part is identified. Remember that DF >+ 0 is only a necessary condition for identification--it is not sufficient.
     Long ago I suggested a little algorithm for hand-counting DF (see attached). For your model, it would work like this:
The  model has 16 observed variables (p = 16), so the number of unique elements in the covariance matrix is:

p*(p+1) / 2 = 136

Then subtract 2p covering observed variable residual variances, loadings and factor variances:

-2p = -32

Subtract 1 for each free covariance (I count 5)

-5

Subtract 1 for every free path between factors (I count 7)

-7

So DF should be 136 - 32 - 5 - 7 = 92.

     I do not know of any simple rule to tell you whether your model with residual covariances for all 4 indicators of previous happiness and happiness will be identified. There was a Bollen and Davis paper from back in the 1980s, but I found that rule itself complicated. Look out for signs of underidentification in your output. It may very well depends on your particular parameter estimates.

Elias,
I do not have any examples to offer.  I would recommend the discussion of residuals in the current edition of Rex Kline's SEM text.  Here is some illustrative code.

# The Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
              auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,
              auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE)
summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE)

# View Residuals (documentation in the lavaan-class help file)
resid(fit, type='raw')
resid(fit, type='cor')
resid(fit, type='normalized')

# Extract unique correlation residuals
fitCorResiduals <- resid(fit, type='cor')$cor
fitCorResidualsUnique <- fitCorResiduals[lower.tri(fitCorResiduals, diag=TRUE)]

# View summary and stem-and-leaf plot
summary(fitCorResidualsUnique)
stem(fitCorResidualsUnique)

# Another plot option
plot(fitCorResidualsUnique[order(fitCorResidualsUnique)], pch=16,
  xlab='', ylab='Correlation Residual')
  abline(h=c(0, -.1, .1), lty=c(1,2,2))

# Flag residuals GT .1 or LT -.1 (choose your own threshold)
flaggedResiduals <- which(abs(fitCorResiduals) > .1, arr.ind=TRUE)

flaggedRowNames <- rownames(fitCorResiduals)[flaggedResiduals[1:5,1]]
flaggedColNames <- colnames(fitCorResiduals)[flaggedResiduals[1:5,2]]
myFlaggedResiduals <- data.frame(flaggedRowNames, flaggedColNames, flaggedValues[1:5])
myResiduals[order(myFlaggedResiduals$flaggedValues),]

messages.body_plain:
Michelle,
   Be careful if you are using fixed.x estimation (possibly by default) because that changes the calculation for the number of unique moments available for df.  Let p be the number of observed variables and x be the number of exogenous observed variables.  If you are only analyzing covariances (not means) then you can compute the number of unique moments as follows.

myMomentCount <- function(p, x=NULL){
  count <- (p * (p + 1)) / 2
  if(!is.null(x)){
    discount <- (x * (x + 1)) / 2
    count <- count  - discount
  }
  return(count)
}
Enter code here...

So, if you are not using fixed.x, then you get 136 moments from 16 variables, as you noted.  Suppose that you had 4 exogenous variables (your model has none).  These 4 variables produce 10 moments.  So, for the purposes of DF, you would count 126 = 136 - 10 if using fixed.x.

I also recommend the following article:
Rigdon, E. E. (1995).  A necessary and sufficient identification rule for structural models estimated in practice.  Multivariate Behavioral Research, 30, 359-383.

messages.body_plain:
Ann,
  I need to answer your question in stages.

(1) Currently, your models are misspecified.  You simulate Cov as an endogenous outcome of the X, M, and Y but you model Cov as an exogenous cause of X, M, and Y.  As a result, your model parameter estimates are biased and you cannot really recover anything accurately.  So, I modified the simulation to match the model.

set.seed(1234)
Cov <- rnorm(100) # changed to exogenous variable
X <- .2 * Cov + rnorm(100)
M <- 0.5 * X + .4 * Cov + rnorm(100)
Y <- 0.7*M + .4 * Cov + rnorm(100)

Data <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y, M = M, Cov=Cov)

(2) I am not clear what you mean by two models for Y.  If you mean that you have two lines beginning "Y ~ " in your model syntax, that is true.  However, you still only have one model (equation) for Y.  Lavaan needs to combine your two lines into one equation for Y.  That is why you cannot duplicate elements across the two lines.

To see this better, look at the matrix form of the model.

> lavInspect(fit, what='free')$beta
    Y M X Cov
Y   0 3 1   2
M   0 0 4   5
X   0 0 0   0
Cov 0 0 0   0

Each element in the matrix represents the effect of the column variable on the row variable.  There is only one parameter for the effect of Cov on Y (labelled 2).  So, you can only specify one parameter to take the place of parameter 2.  Likewise, there is only one row in the table for Y.  That row represents the one and only equation for Y in the model.

(3) Yes, I believe that it would be possible to compute those things as defined parameters.  However, the variances of endogenous variables are not parameters in the model.  So, you would first need to compute those as defined parameters.  You could then use those to compute the variance passed on through a given effect.  Finally, you could take the ratios of these to obtain something analogous to an R-square.

However, I am not sure how useful that would be.  If I am thinking about this correctly, the variances of X and Y will just cancel out of the numerator and denominator.  So, you could just look at the ratios formed from squaring the effects.

model <- ' # Duplicate label omitted

# X and Y
X ~ Cov
Y ~ c*X + d*Cov + b*M

# mediator
M ~ a*X + e*Cov

# indirect effect (a*b)
ab := a*b

abSquare := ab^2

# total effect
total := c + (a*b)

cSquare := c^2

# proportions
abProp := abSquare / (abSquare + cSquare)
cProp := cSquare / (abSquare + cSquare)

' # End model syntax

fit <- sem(model, data = Data)

summary(fit)

Here is the result for the two proportions.

    abProp            0.906    0.164    5.507    0.000
    cProp             0.094    0.164    0.574    0.566

I have never seen that done before.  So, perhaps others can chime in if I am missing something.

Keith

Faiz--
     Yes, the software will compute the necessary moments (covariance matrix and means, if necesary) in the background, when you supply the data. There are statistical reasons why it is better to provide the data itself, rather than giving lavaan a covariance matrix only. And there is, generally, no advantage in providing only a covariance matrix. The exception might be when sample size is very large, and you expect to run several different models. Then you might save computing time by computing the covariance matrix once (using the R cov() function, for example), instead of having lavaan compute it each tim a model is run.
Ed Rigdon

messages.body_plain:
lavaan is not a good exploratory tool--it will not find the correct model for you.
You have to specify the set of equations that you want to estimate.
Let's say that X1 and X3 have direct effects on Y, and X5 and X6 have *only* indirect effects through X1 and X3. That means that X1 and X3 are dependent on X5 and X6. So there will be three structural model equations, one each for Y, X1 and X3:

Y ~ X1 + X3
X1 ~ X5 + X6
X3 + X5 + X6

You could put the second and third equations together as:
X1 + X3 ~ X5 + X6

Remember, in factor-based SEM, there is one equation for each dependent variable. With lavaan, you may break that one equation up into multiple lines, like:
Y ~ X1
Y ~ X3

messages.subject: Re: Question about data simulation
messages.subject_clean: Question about data simulation
messages.body_plain:
Diya,
  Your examples are overly complex for your question.  Here is a simple example to illustrate the concepts.  You can then apply the concepts to your more complex models.

  Suppose that you have one unmeasured latent variable that affects one measured latent variable with three indicators and that two observed covaraites have direct effects on the observed indicators.  Here is a way to simulate data from such a model.

# Simulate model with unmeasured latent observed covaraites

require(lavaan)

simModelSyntax <- '
  # Measurement Models (latent variables)
  unmeasuredLatent =~ 0
  measuredLatent =~ 1*x1 + .9*x2 + .8*x3     # indicators x1 to x3

  # Regressions
  measuredLatent ~ .5*unmeasuredLatent
  x1 ~ .5*c1 + -.5*c2                        # covariates c1 and c2

  # Variances and disturbances
  unmeasuredLatent ~~ 1*unmeasuredLatent
  measuredLatent ~~ .5*measuredLatent
  x1 ~~ .3*x1
  x2 ~~ .3*x2
  x3 ~~ .3*x3
  c1 ~~ 1*c1
  c2 ~~ 1*c2

  # Covariances
  c1 ~~ .5*c2
' # End model syntax

myData <- simulateData(model=simModelSyntax, sample.nobs=1000)
head(myData)
round(cov(myData),3) # covariance matrix rounded for viewing

Note that the input to lavaan is just the data for the observed variables.  Were it otherwise, there would be no meaningful distinction between observed and unobserved variables.  As such, the simulated data will not include values for the two latent variables.  If you have an unmeasured latent variable that affects to other latent variables, you could also simulate this as an unexplained covariance between the two variables.  An unmeasured latent variable that has no effects on any other variable in the model, such as in your second example, can be omitted entirely form the simulation because it does not impact the observed variables.

If you want to simulate data for latent variables, then change the model syntax to treat them as observed variables.

Also, as a general rule, a path diagram should represent every parameter in the algebraic model.  Your diagrams are not strictly speaking path diagrams because they omit variances and disturbances.  Explicit representation of the algebraic model is one thing that distinguishes path diagrams from more abstract graphical representations such as causal graphs and logic models.

HTH,
Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: Re: Residual Analysis
messages.subject_clean: Residual Analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hi Elias,

The primary advantage to using residuals is to identify local areas of poor fit that might be hidden or obscured by global summary statistics.  It may be that most of a model fits well but parts fit poorly.  Identifying high residuals may offer hints for model respecification.

One advantage to correlation residuals is that it is easier to formulate criteria for practical significance.  As explained in the lavaan-class help file (use the help(' . . .') idom, not the ?. . . shortcut), the standardized residuals are like z scores.  The normalized residuals are less apt to generate NAs.  To avoid alpha inflation, you may want to adopt a more conservative rule than .05.  Rex Kline's 4th edition of his SEM book offers an excellent overview of model fit assessment.  The above help file also includes a reference with more detailed information about residuals.  Remember that other fit statistics and indices offer a supplement to chi-square rather than a replacement.

Keith

messages.subject_clean: Modification indices using measurement invariance
messages.body_plain:
On Friday, January 12, 2018 at 6:51:15 PM UTC+1, Ashly Westrick wrote:
>
> Hello. I am currently doing a multigroup CFA on a quality of life instrument between English and Spanish speakers. I am doing this analysis in R using the lavaan package. I am also new to this type of analysis. I found that measurement invariance is violated between the metric and configural models and would like to investigate which loadings are causing the violations. I came across the lavtestscore() function and was using this however I am unsure how to interpret the output. Below is an example of the output for one of my domains.
>
>
>
>  <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-9YKhfMJDsFw/Wlj1XyaiVdI/AAAAAAAADX4/7lst9GzJYEIds08kt_KNc7DQTlwDKz8ZgCLcBGAs/s1600/Screen%2BShot%2B2018-01-12%2Bat%2B12.49.58%2BPM.png>
>
>
>
> I have read that an epc greater than 0.1 you would consider releasing. How do I interpret these other values (ets, epv).

"est" is short  for "estimate" (the current estimated value in the fitted model). EPC stands for expected parameter change, and EPV stands for expected parameter value (the sum of "est" and "epc").   So EPV is the best guess at what the value would be if you were to simultaneously free the all of the constraint indicated in the $uni portion of the lavTestScore() output.  This behavior differs from the modindices() function, which makes the simplifying assumptions that (1) you only want to free 1 fixed parameter, and that (2) you only want to know how much that specific parameter would change (from its fixed value) if you freely estimated that specific parameter.

lavTestScore() is much more flexible, at the cost of being simple:
By default, it considers all parameter constraints, NOT fixed parameters (unless you fix a parameter by labeling it in your model syntax and specify in the model syntax that it is equal to a particular value)
It returns a total test statistic (in the $test portion of the output) for freeing all of those constraints, in addition to test statistics for each individual constraint
If requested, it will return expected parameter changes (and values) for all estimated model parameters, assuming ALL constraints were released
The behavior of modindices() can be mimicked by using the add= argument to obtain tests (and EPCs) for if a fixed parameter(s) were freely estimated.  See the ?lavTestScore help page for details and an example.

You can call lavTestScore() as you already do if you are only interested in those test statistics.  But if you also want to see how much estimated parameters change when only 1 constraint is freed (or the set of constraints associated with one loading across more than 2 groups), then you must use the release= argument to release that/those constraint(s), one (set) at a time.  Then you will see one $uni test statistic at a time (same as you already see all at once), but the EPCs will reflect expectations if only that (set of) constraint(s) were freed.  Here is an example, based on the ?cfa help page:

example(cfa)
## fit a metric-invariance model
fitmg <- update(fit, group = "school", group.equal = "loadings")
## save the full parameter table
PT <- parTable(fitmg)
## print the part with loadings (to see labels) and constraints (to test)
PT[PT$op %in% c("=~","=="), ]
## pass the numbers (in the order they appear in the full PT) of the
## 6 constraints you want to test (i.e., 1:6) one at a time to lavTestScore()
lavTestScore(fitmg, release = 1, epc = TRUE)
lavTestScore(fitmg, release = 2, epc = TRUE)
...
lavTestScore(fitmg, release = 6, epc = TRUE)

Note that this also allows you to see how much OTHER model parameters (potentially of greater interest) would change if a loading were unconstrained.  Specifically, constraining loadings allows factor variances to be freely estimated in all but 1 group (unless they already were because you fix the first loading to 1, as in the example above -- but that identification method assumes the first loading per factor IS INVARIANT without testing that assumption, so I recommend fixing factor variances to 1 for identification, then freeing all but one group's once loadings are constrained across groups).  So if you want to see the (expected) impact of a loading-constraint on the estimated factor variance, then look for that EPC in the output as well.  The "EPC-interest" method for model evaluation/respecification was recently proposed by Daniel Oberski in a few papers:

dx.doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpt014 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpt014>

dx.doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpv020 <http://dx.doi.org/10.1093/pan/mpv020>

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

On Monday, January 8, 2018 at 11:52:47 AM UTC-5, kma...@aol.com wrote:
> Ann,
>   I need to answer your question in stages.
>
> (1) Currently, your models are misspecified.  You simulate Cov as an endogenous outcome of the X, M, and Y but you model Cov as an exogenous cause of X, M, and Y.  As a result, your model parameter estimates are biased and you cannot really recover anything accurately.  So, I modified the simulation to match the model.
>
> set.seed(1234)
> Cov <- rnorm(100) # changed to exogenous variable
> X <- .2 * Cov + rnorm(100)
> M <- 0.5 * X + .4 * Cov + rnorm(100)
> Y <- 0.7*M + .4 * Cov + rnorm(100)
> Data <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y, M = M, Cov=Cov)
>
>
>
> (2) I am not clear what you mean by two models for Y.  If you mean that you have two lines beginning "Y ~ " in your model syntax, that is true.  However, you still only have one model (equation) for Y.  Lavaan needs to combine your two lines into one equation for Y.  That is why you cannot duplicate elements across the two lines.
>
> To see this better, look at the matrix form of the model.
>
> > lavInspect(fit, what='free')$beta
>     Y M X Cov
> Y   0 3 1   2
> M   0 0 4   5
> X   0 0 0   0
> Cov 0 0 0   0
>
> Each element in the matrix represents the effect of the column variable on the row variable.  There is only one parameter for the effect of Cov on Y (labelled 2).  So, you can only specify one parameter to take the place of parameter 2.  Likewise, there is only one row in the table for Y.  That row represents the one and only equation for Y in the model.
>
> (3) Yes, I believe that it would be possible to compute those things as defined parameters.  However, the variances of endogenous variables are not parameters in the model.  So, you would first need to compute those as defined parameters.  You could then use those to compute the variance passed on through a given effect.  Finally, you could take the ratios of these to obtain something analogous to an R-square.
>
> However, I am not sure how useful that would be.  If I am thinking about this correctly, the variances of X and Y will just cancel out of the numerator and denominator.  So, you could just look at the ratios formed from squaring the effects.
>
> model <- ' # Duplicate label omitted
>
> # X and Y
> X ~ Cov
> Y ~ c*X + d*Cov + b*M
>
> # mediator
> M ~ a*X + e*Cov
>
> # indirect effect (a*b)
> ab := a*b
> abSquare := ab^2
>
> # total effect
> total := c + (a*b)
> cSquare := c^2
>
> # proportions
> abProp := abSquare / (abSquare + cSquare)
> cProp := cSquare / (abSquare + cSquare)
>
> ' # End model syntax
>
>
> fit <- sem(model, data = Data)
> summary(fit)
>
> Here is the result for the two proportions.
>
>     abProp            0.906    0.164    5.507    0.000
>     cProp             0.094    0.164    0.574    0.566
>
> I have never seen that done before.  So, perhaps others can chime in if I am missing something.
>
> Keith
> ------------------------
> Keith A. Markus
> John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
> http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
> Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
> http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/
>

messages.subject: Re: SEM - modindices
messages.subject_clean: SEM - modindices
messages.body_plain:
This is an R problem - R is looking for a chunk of contiguous memory and it can't find it in your computer.  You might try rebooting your computer, and making sure you're not running any other programs (temporarily turn off your virus scanner, etc).

Alternatively, you can reduce the amount of memory needed. That's a big chunk of memory. Can you simplify your model or your data? E.g. if you're running MLR, run ML instead. If you've got missing data, do listwise deletion, don't use FIML. If your data set is large, resample it in half.

Your modification indices should still be in the correct ballpark if you do those things, even if they're not identical.

Jeremy

messages.subject: Satisfactory absolute fit indices, but low CFI and TLI
messages.subject_clean: Satisfactory absolute fit indices, but low CFI and TLI
messages.body_plain:
Dear all.

I'm trying to run a two-level CFA model, where a questionnaire of 52 items is loaded on 7 subscales, which are further loaded on 2 second-order factors. We have a sample of ~1200 participants. Whereas the RMSEA is 0.055, and the SRMR is 0.06, the CFI and TLI are ~0.83. Following the suggestion of Kenny (http://davidakenny.net/cm/fit.htm) I've tested the RMSEA of the null model which turned out to be 0.14 (which is smaller than 0.158, which Kenny suggests to indicate that "an incremental measure of fit may not be that informative"). I understand that this means that the correlations between items are not that high. I assume it has a lot to do with the fact the it is a highly multidimensional questionnaire, where some of the factors are indeed not so related (conceptually and statistically) to the other factors.
My question is - can this situation still count as a reasonable fit (and can it thus be published?). Also - does anyone knows of any academic papers discussing such a divergence between absolute and relative fit indices, and supporting Kenny's suggestion (which he only published in his website but not in an academic paper)?
Thanks!
Issac

messages.body_plain:
Elias,
  I suppose that you could bootstrap the desired standard errors and then divide the raw residuals by the resulting standard error estimates.  You can use '/' to divide each element in a matrix by the corresponding element of a matrix of equal dimensions.

> A <- matrix(seq(2,8,by=2), ncol=2, nrow=2)
> B <- matrix(2, ncol=2, nrow=2)
> A
     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    2    6
[2,]    4    8
> B
     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    2    2
[2,]    2    2
> A / B
     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    3
[2,]    2    4
>

Bear in mind that you are performing multiple tests.  So, alpha = .05 may not serve you well with standardized or normalized residuals.  Personally, I prefer to simply place the correlation residuals into a stem-and-leaf plot and look for outliers or residuals above a size that I deem practically significant.

Keith

messages.subject: Re: Standardized Residuals for DWLS in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Standardized Residuals for DWLS in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Here is a more fleshed out illustration of what I meant.

# The Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939,
              auto.var=TRUE, auto.fix.first=TRUE,
              auto.cov.lv.x=TRUE)
summary(fit, fit.measures=TRUE)

rawResiduals <- residuals(fit, type='raw')
rawResiduals
class(rawResiduals$cov)

madeUpSEs <- matrix(.01, ncol=9, nrow=9) # in practice you would bootstrap these

rawResiduals$cov / madeUpSEs # This is how you could compute standardized or normalized residuals.

Normalized and standardized residuals are like z scores.  So, if you interpret each one as a separate z test, then you invite alpha inflation.

I do not know how to point to a specific post but see my January 7 post in response to your thread entitled "Chi-square result for large sample size and normed chi-square".  that post contains sample code for graphing residuals.

Keith

messages.body_plain:
The reason you dont have fit measures is because your models are saturaded. This means that you are estimating as many relations as information from the covariance matrix. This is shown by having df=0. When you have df=0 you cannot estimate fit

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

in order to avoid heywood cases, I also would like to fix the error variances of the observed variables so that they are positive (i.e., > 0).

First, I tried the first solution proposed above with var > 0 and var < 1 with the following model syntax:

m1 <- 'inhib =~ antisaccade + stopsignal + colorstroop + simon + numberstroop + arrowflanker

                # constraints

                antisaccade ~~ b1*antisaccade

                stopsignal ~~ b2*stopsignal

                colorstroop ~~ b3*colorstroop

                simon ~~ b4*simon

                numberstroop ~~ b5*numberstroop

                arrowflanker ~~ b6*arrowflanker

                b1 > 0

                b2 > 0

                b3 > 0

                b4 > 0

                b5 > 0

                b6 > 0

b1 < 1

                b2 < 1

                b3 < 1

                b4 < 1

                b5 < 1

b6 < 1'

fit <- sem(m1, data=d, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

This model had bad fit statistics and strange indices (e.g., CFI = 0, RMSEA = 9.92, SRMR = 0.47), and all estimates for the error variances were 1.

Second, I tried a model with only var > 0, with the following code:

m2 <- 'inhib =~ antisaccade + stopsignal + colorstroop + simon + numberstroop + arrowflanker

                # constraints

                antisaccade ~~ b1*antisaccade

                stopsignal ~~ b2*stopsignal

                colorstroop ~~ b3*colorstroop

                simon ~~ b4*simon

                numberstroop ~~ b5*numberstroop

                arrowflanker ~~ b6*arrowflanker

                b1 > 0

                b2 > 0

                b3 > 0

                b4 > 0

                b5 > 0

                b6 > 0'

fit <- sem(m2, data=d, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

This model had good fit statistics, but with the warning that some estimated ov variances are negative. Therefore, it doesn’t seem to work.

Third, I tried a model in which all error variances were fixed to a particular value (i.e., 0.001).

m2 <- 'inhib =~ antisaccade + stopsignal + colorstroop + simon + numberstroop + arrowflanker

                # constraints

                antisaccade ~~ 0.001

                stopsignal ~~ 0.001

                colorstroop ~~ 0.001

                simon ~~ 0.001

                numberstroop ~~ 0.001

                arrowflanker ~~ 0.001'

fit <- sem(m3, data=d, std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE)

But, logically, I got the error message that they were missing observed variables in dataset: ..constant..

As my data are not categorical, and the parametrization is currently used only for categorical data, this doesn’t seem to be the solution either.

Therefore: Is there a way to constraint all variances of the observed variables to be positive or at least to fix them to a particular value?

Thanks in advance for your response!

Alodie

messages.body_plain:
Alodie,
(1) The constraints are on the unstandardized solution.  So, there is no guarantee that the unique variances are less than one.  So, one likely hypothesis is that they are all greater than 1 and restricting them to 1 in the first model led them all to land at the ceiling.  In this case, the fit measures may not be odd at all, but rather accurately reflecting the horrible fit to the data (not noticeably better than the baseline model).

(2) Attempting to use constraints to avoid Heywood cases is a controversial strategy (it was one issue that separated LISREL from EQS back in the day).  The reason is that Heywood cases often result from model misspecification.  If you constrain the estimates, the misspecification does not go away.  Your problematic estimates of latent variable variances in the second model may simply result from the same underlying misspecification manifesting itself in a new way.

(3) If you want to use constraints to avoid Heywood cases, the canonical EQS strategy was to fix the unique variances to unity but freely estimate the loading for the unique variance.  The loading is not bounded at either end.  So, everything is in bounds.  Lavaan is based on Mplus which in turn was based on LISREL.  So, each of these inherits the LISREL strategy of fixing the loading and estimating the variance.  Therefore, to adopt the EQS strategy, you need to not only fix the unique variance (fix, not constrain) but also to introduce a loading parameter because the LISREL model makes these implicit.  One way to do this is to fix the default unique variances to zero and introduce new latent variables with unit variances to serve as unique variances.

(4) When you fix a variance to a specific value, you still need to multiply that value by the variable name on the right hand side of the ~~ operator.  You omitted that in your code for the third model.

HTH,
Keith

John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus

messages.subject: Re: How to measure Latent means?
messages.subject_clean: How to measure Latent means?
messages.body_plain:
There are multiple methods.  Here is one.  See a SEM text such as Kline (2016) for details.

# Reference group method
require(lavaan)

HS.model <- '
  visual =~ c(l1, l1) * x1 + c(l2, l2) * x2 + c(l3, l3) * x3       # CFA model with loadings constrained across groups
  visual ~~ c(1, NA) * visual                                      # fix latent variable variance in first group
  visual ~ c(0, NA) * 1                                            # constrain latent variable mean to 1 in first group
  x1 ~~ x1
  x2 ~~ x2
  x3 ~~ x3
  x1 ~ c(v1, v1) * 1                                               # constrain intercepts across groups
  x2 ~ c(v2, v2) * 1
  x3 ~ c(v3, v3) * 1
' # end model syntax

fit <- lavaan(HS.model,
              data = HolzingerSwineford1939,
              group = "school")                                    # specify two-group analysis

summary(fit)

For a statistical test, rerun the model with both latent variable means set to zero and then inspect the chi-square difference test.

------------------------

messages.subject_clean: fixing error variances from 0 to 1
messages.body_plain:
Alodie,
When you see that error, you can use either of the following (or both) to investigate your model specification.

lavaanify(fit)
lavInspect(fit, what='free')

You missed some steps in implementing the EQS strategy.  The df should match your original model because you are just moving parameters around.

# The Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
HS.model <- '
  visual =~ 1*x1 + x2 + x3  # Define common factor
  x1 ~~ 0*x1                # Zero out default unique variances
  x2 ~~ 0*x2
  x3 ~~ 0*x3
  u1 =~ 0                   # Define new latent variables for unique variances
  u2 =~ 0
  u3 =~ 0
  visual ~~ visual          # factor variance freely estimated
  u1 ~~ 1*u1                # unique variances fixed to one
  u2 ~~ 1*u2
  u3 ~~ 1*u3
  x1 ~ start(1)*u1          # Estimate loadings for unique variances
  x2 ~ start(1)*u2          # The need for start values may be sample specific
  x3 ~ start(1)*u3
' # end model syntax

fit <- lavaan(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)

summary(fit)

Remember that constraints will not help you find the cause of the Heywood case.  Look through the list archive for various posts by Terrence Jorgensen describing ruling out the hypothesis that the Heywood case is due to sampling error.

The EQS type model is very similar to your 2nd model constraining the unique variances to be positive.  The difference is that this model does the equivalent of constraining them to be non-negative.  The chi-square values should be nearly identical.

Keith

messages.subject: Translating jags likelihood into Lavaan model
messages.subject_clean: Translating jags likelihood into Lavaan model
messages.body_plain:
I’m having trouble translating a model written in jags into R code.

I’m trying to explain the effects of betaTreat on y measured at the site level, where betaTreat is 3 levels of x (low/medium/high), which can vary through time, and are measured at the quadrat level.

The basic jags likelihood looks something like this:

# likelihood

##  y at the site-level affected by betaTreat

for(i in 1:n){

  y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], tau.site)

 mu[i] <- alpha + betaTreat[treat[i]]

}

##  x at the quadrat-level represented by quadrat-level measures of x

for(q in 1:nq){

  x[q] ~ dnorm(x.mu <http://x.mu>[q], tau.quad)

  x.mu <http://x.mu>[q] <- betaTreat[qtreat[q]] + betaTime * time[q]

}

I would like to develop this model in R, because its faster and easier now and later, but have been unable to do this using ‘lmer’.

I was wondering whether betaTreat might be considered a latent variable, estimated by quadrat-level measurements of x, and if so, whether this likelihood could be written as a ‘lavaan’ model?

Thanks for any help,

Jess

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

If you are working with observed variables, that is the way to go. See e.g.

Dawson, J. F. (2014). Moderation in Management Research: What, Why, When, and How. Journal of Business and Psychology, 29(1), 1–19. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10869-013-9308-7

If you have moderation between latent variables, then things get a bit more trickier. I recommend taking a look at Kline’s book first.

Kline, R. B. (2011). Principles and practice of structural equation modeling (3rd ed.). New York, NY: Guilford Press.

Mikko
